utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At about 200 -- paragraph 208, Mr. Deronjic, you deal with the arrival in Srebrenica of a man called Beara who you understood to be the man spoken of by Karadzic, and his instructions in relation to the prisoners were to the effect that what should happen to them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you give me the number of the paragraph again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 209, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that paragraph I spoke about the arrival of Mr. Beara in Bratunac, I would say, because I'm not sure whether he had been to Srebrenica. I spoke about the fact that he came to my office late at night between the 13th and the 14th of July. It is a well-known fact, and I mentioned it in my statement, that on the 13th, at night, I talked to Mr. Karadzic, and the transcript of that conversation is precisely the document which we read from a moment ago. Mr. Beara showed up at my office on the 13th in the evening, and in this paragraph I described in detail the atmosphere in my office and the orders he related to me regarding the Muslim prisoners who at the time were located in the municipality of Bratunac. Do you need any further details on this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. It's in the statement, and people can read what his instructions were. And then finally in paragraph 227, you deal with the document with which the Chamber is very familiar because it's been recently produced. That's the document dealing with the apparently, or so said to be, legitimate and proper evacuation of people from Srebrenica. It's the document Mr. Franken signed, having amended it. You deal with that document in paragraph 226 and 227, and you say that the document did not correspond with reality. And if you'll go right to the end of paragraph 227, we can read all the reasons why it didn't correspond to reality if necessary, but you say finally the main reason or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the basic reason for that document not corresponding with reality was what, please, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I said that the main reason was that there was no real intention to allow that population, and I mean now the civilians who found themselves in the base in Potocari after we captured Srebrenica, to remain there. All the preceding events and this event itself confirm my theory which I may have explained earlier, namely that the Muslim population should be cleared from that area, eliminated from that area. That was the real intention. And the instructions I had received did not coincide with the reality. And I am referring now to the options that I was instructed to convey to the Muslims on behalf of President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, thank you very much. You'll be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the audio -- I beg your pardon, the intercept that the accused asked about, this is one of those for which we do not have an audio version. We have the hard copy, and it will be production of the hard copy that will be dealt with in later evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's now for you to cross-examine the witness. We've considered the time which you should have available, and we think you should have two and a half hours to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't understand how you can allocate to me only two and a half hours for a witness who is for all practical purposes not a live testimony witness, who comes in with a statement containing 232 paragraphs, or in other words 232 different assertions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which means that I am supposed to cover 100 paragraphs per hour, including all this documentation. It is completely impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Get on with the cross-examination. Don't waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to waste any time, but can I establish first what kind of transcript is it which is not accompanied by an audio recording? What is it a transcript of then? I'm talking about this conversation between Deronjic and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the moment, the exhibit has purely been marked for identification. We will decide in due course whether to admit it. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Deronjic, first of all I would ask you a few introductory questions, background questions that have to do with your assertion you made a moment ago in response to a question by Mr. Nice, namely that you drew your conclusions about the events in question in 1997 at the time of your contacts with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is not what I said. I said that for the most part, I drew my conclusions during the war, and some conclusions I drew after the war was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you did mention the side opposite and your contacts with them starting with 1997, and you said that in 1997, you arrived at some sort of version of your own about the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that connection, I would like you to clarify a few things for me. I have in front of me the agreement that you concluded with the Prosecution, your plea agreement. I suppose that you are familiar with it. You concluded a plea agreement with the side opposite; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no time to go through this entire document, but I will refer to some things contained in it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, gentlemen, that you have this agreement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We do not. We do not, but we will have it available.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters say they don't have this agreement either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can make one copy available to the Bench straight away, I have one other copy of my own, if we can get the others copied, then the shortfall will be remedied as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that plea agreement you concluded with the Office of the Prosecutor, from what I can see with regard to the key part of your testimony, they are not charging you with anything related to Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Interpretation of the agreement on the part of the Prosecutor." That's what it says. "Based on complete and significant cooperation of Mr. Deronjic with the Prosecution, the Prosecution will recommend to the Chamber to determine a sentence of ten years." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: B reads: "The Prosecution will undertake the necessary and reasonable measures to ensure complete safety to Miroslav Deronjic and his family." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It reads on: "Based on this plea agreement, Miroslav Deronjic assumes complete responsibility for his criminal acts in the village of Glogova." That is, it reduces your responsibility to events in Glogova; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on, point D, it says: "Regarding the criminal responsibility of Miroslav Deronjic for all other criminal acts he could be charged with regarding events in Glogova on the 9th of May, 1992, as described in the charges in the second amended indictment, the Prosecution will inform the competent national courts that these acts have been dealt with." In other words, they should not prosecute you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It goes on to say regarding events in Glogova on the 9th of May, 1992, as described and so on and so forth in the second amendment indictment: "The Prosecutor will --" I am warned by the interpreters that they do not have the document so I will read more slowly. "The Prosecutor will inform national courts that this particular act falls under the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Tribunal." Correct, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, since we are dealing here with the second amended indictment, in what way is it different from the first amended indictment, Mr. Deronjic, or simply first indictment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: How is it different? Well, I cannot tell you precisely what the differences are because I don't have the text in front of me, but it is different, certainly, from the first one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The difference is, I suppose, that it reduces your responsibility to Glogova, and you are promised a sentence of ten years. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the first indictment against me related only to Glogova, exclusively to Glogova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Deronjic. We have a sub-heading "Cooperation by Mr. Deronjic. He commits himself to meet with the representatives of the Prosecution as often as necessary and provide them with the necessary information related to the well-known events in the former Yugoslavia." It goes on to say that: "Miroslav Deronjic agrees to testify truthfully at any trial, at any hearing, in any other proceeding before the International Tribunal where, in the opinion of the Prosecutor, his testimony could be relevant be it a current case in front of the Tribunal or any future case." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, your testimony is based on this plea agreement you made with the Prosecution. Is that correct, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It is correct, Mr. Milosevic. However, I will tell you a couple of things that you don't know. During my first contacts with the Office of the Prosecutor - and this can be confirmed by my Defence counsel - I said that even if I never make a plea agreement, I will testify in front of this Tribunal. I don't have the text in front of me, but you can check that with my lawyers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no intention of doing anything of the kind. In this second amended indictment which refers only to Glogova --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milosevic. Even the first indictment, and I've said this already, relates only to the events in Glogova, and I would like to say this again on record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Deronjic. My point is not the coverage of the indictment, my point is your plea agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor whereby they take it upon themselves to recommend to the Trial Chamber to sentence you to ten years; and that is the basis on which you concluded this agreement, isn't it, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Inter alia, this recommended sentence is an element of the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as other elements such as protection measures, relief from Prosecution in national courts, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know that this honourable Tribunal gives priority to the Prosecution of persons guilty of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia. I don't see anything wrong with the same formulation being used in my case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know what the priorities are of this so-called Tribunal, but let us move on to your actual testimony which is based on this plea agreement with the Office of the Prosecutor. Let us move on in accordance with the main events involved. I don't know exactly how much time I will get eventually, but first I'm going to deal with Srebrenica in 1995. In paragraph 161 of your statement, you say that you often talked to Karadzic on the subject of Srebrenica. And as you say about the presence of international forces, relations with these forces personnel matters, personnel issues with the army, military issues, and so on and so forth. Is that right, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of all these frequent conversations and exchanges of opinions, you must have been very well aware of Karadzic's views of Srebrenica even before 1995 and what happened then.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: To the extent to which Mr. Karadzic had the intention of telling me openly about his intentions, so I know what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that since you talked frequently and you were the person who was in charge of Srebrenica that you had to be aware of all these positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It is absolutely not right. If there are secret plans and if the president does not deem it necessary to tell me about this, then he's not going to tell me. At any rate, I can confirm that I was aware of some plans related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Therefore, it seems that you were not aware of his positions in Srebrenica, because otherwise you would have spoken about them in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had heard of some plans. I don't know how objective and truthful they are, and that's what I said to the Office of the Prosecutor in my extensive statement. I said that there were some stories to the effect that it would be possible that Srebrenica would be exchanged for some territory within the federation. I did hear of such plans in these conversations, but I don't know how objective this was and how possible this was at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Some concrete talks that you had about Srebrenica with Karadzic that you mention. I assume that you did not mention all of them in this statement. You provide the information that in your opinion has to do with your own behaviour there and the events that have to do with you yourself. This conversation took place when Karadzic once came to Zvornik, and you say it's spring. It's the spring of 1995 or perhaps the month of May; is that right? Then you say that he took you to the side and that Karadzic told you then that in Srebrenica some military operation would be taking place but he did not give you any details.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's right. He said that to me, among other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that he told you about that already then, he told you that you shouldn't talk to anyone about this.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that he had great confidence in you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I assumed that he had confidence in me too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then he asked you that upon your return to Bratunac you should take the measures that you deem necessary in relation to this military operation, that he only hinted at, if I understood this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what were the preparatory measures that you took in relation to this military operation that he had hinted at to you upon your return to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I explained this in one particular paragraph. These were routine actions that were customary in preparation of military operations. I checked whether we had among our reserves sufficient quantities of oil, then also whether there was enough medicine at the health centre and also whether we had sufficient food supplies at the time, and I asked the municipal leadership to prepare this if they realised that there wasn't enough of any of these materials. I said that there would be something going on in connection with Srebrenica and that we should be ready, too, as we did several times before that when operations took place in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you say yourself that you did not know anything about these operations in greater detail, how could you on the basis of such scant information know what were the quantities involved in relation to all these supplies? What did you actually have to prepare and how much?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: We never knew what the necessary quantities were. We made an effort to have optimum quantities in relation to the possibilities that the municipality had. For example, if in that area there is going to be a military operation, then it is necessary for us to have a large transportation company there. It is necessary to suggest to people that they should have as many oil reserves as possible and also that the municipality should make an effort to set up oil reserves. Of course we never had any idea how much would be necessary. Oil supplies come through military channels as well, but very often during this war the municipality assisted the military, and I can give you countless number of examples to this effect, and I can say that the municipality bought some food supplies, oil reserves, et cetera, everything that was of priority importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Deronjic, did you report to Karadzic in the meantime at all about preparations carried out to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. Even in the previous period in relation to these activities that are normal for the civilian authorities in this area, there was no practice of informing the leadership of Republika Srpska about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So Karadzic could not have known what he could count on in Bratunac if this operation that he hinted at was to take place.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: He could absolutely count on the preparations that were supposed to be carried out by the military, and from that point of view he probably had that information made accessible to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But since you say that you did not report about your preparations, then this could not have made it possible for him to count on you in relation to the tasks that you carried out.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, no, not really but then he could have known that I acted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. within the scope of the material possibilities of the municipality and that I did whatever I could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 164, you say that these preparations that you took care of were not something that caused spectacular interest among the population because you were not involved in the military aspect of the preparation for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: The first part is contained in that paragraph first and foremost. I said that these were routine actions, and I said that when the units arrived in the second half of June in that area, and then the command of these units and the reconnaissance that took place, et cetera, all of this did not cause any spectacular interest among the ordinary people because such operations had taken place in the previous period as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that although you said that you talked to Karadzic about this operation from the very beginning but that you did not really talk to anyone else about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the military operation regarding Srebrenica start in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure when the action actually started. The first days of the month of July, I believe. But some activities started already in the second half of June. I cannot say exactly and I was not involved in them but there were some activities of the military that were noticeable in the second half of June. Specifically, I think that the Srebrenica action started in the first days of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is my understanding on the basis of what you say in paragraph 167 that as a matter of fact during the first days when the operation started, you did not even go towards Srebrenica, as you said yourself, in order to see for yourself what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This does say the month of July. Perhaps during the first two or three days in the month of July. That's the period I meant when I said that I did not go in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in paragraph 168 you say that on the 1st of July, or perhaps a day or two before that --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say on the 1st of July or perhaps a day or two before that, so then perhaps on the 29th or 30th of June, you went to the forward command post at Pribicevac and that is the first time you briefly saw General Krstic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I said because I cannot remember exactly the date when I was present myself at Pribicevac. That is why I said the 1st of July, a day or two before that, or perhaps a day or two after that. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how is that possible when in the previous paragraph, 167, you say that during the first days you did not go anywhere from Bratunac and that you were only guessing that this was fighting for the road between Skelani and Milici.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean that it's not possible? I said that the preparations of the military in that area started in the second half of the month of June, certain activities of the army. So I did not take part in this, and I was not present myself during these activities. When I went to Pribicevac, and that has to do with those days approximately, I cannot exactly remember, then I saw for myself what the activities were like in the actual area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Since you say that on that occasion you had a brief meeting with General Krstic, tell me, what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. I said that this meeting was a very brief one, I said that I met Mr. Krstic at Pribicevac during those days in the month of July. I spoke to him briefly, I introduced myself to him, I said who I was and what I did, and nothing special. I didn't discuss anything special with him because he was busy issuing certain orders in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you just said hello to him and you didn't really talk.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I cannot remember very precisely. These are events that took place a long time ago. I explained that there was this table in front of this forward command post, perhaps we sat down and had a cup of coffee. I personally did not know Mr. Krstic, and he had not known me either. This was a courtesy talk. I did not want to be a hindrance in any way and I cannot say how long this lasted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 170 you say that one day you went to the actual combat site on the south side of Pribicevac where you say the actual military operation was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which day did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly which days these were. It was these days in July, and I cannot say exactly whether it was the 10th. Perhaps it was the 10th, the 7th, the 6th of July. I cannot say exactly because at this point in time it's not quite clear to me when the military part of the operation started, but that is where I saw the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. I said hello to him, and I saw directly how these operations around Srebrenica were evolving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, you say that you saw the commander of the Drina Wolves at the time, whose nickname was Legenda, the Legend.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I remember that I saw Vinko Pandurevic, and I saw this man whose nickname was Legenda. I didn't know his real name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you talk to him then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I can explain this quite accurately. This is a trench where they were, a communicating trench -- communication trench towards -- facing a locality on the other side. During the actual operation while these elevations were being taken, they are called the three tits, that's what they're called in that area. I did not stay for very long there. I just said hello to Mr. Pandurevic and I realised that he was in a great hurry and that this operation was already under way and whether it continued later, I really don't know about these details, because I did not stay long there and I went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Deronjic. As for General Krstic or this Legenda or Pandurevic, so these men who are officers, commanders within the command that was involved in the operation, you did not ask any one of them about the objectives of the operation. You simply inferred your own conclusions; you did not get any information from them.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, not knowing about the goals of that military operation, you decided then to seek your own information from Radovan Karadzic directly and to suggest to him to involve a special police unit of the MUP of Republika Srpska commanded by Ljubisa Borovcanin and to have them involved in all this. That's what you say in paragraph 171; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, why did you get this idea, this military idea, if I can put it this way? You say that you were layman and that you didn't know anything about this, and so how did you get this idea that Borovcanin's special unit should be involved in all this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in my statement I explained in greater detail that as I spent time during the first half of July at this particular place that is called Pribicevac, I visited the units of the Bratunac Brigade that were for the most part deployed in that area. And I spent one night or even more in the area talking to people about various things, of course, but we were mostly interested in the plan regarding Srebrenica, and people were asking me about the plans, the military plans that had to do with Srebrenica that they were taking direct part in. So this was one of the motives involved. And I told the men that I would see how I could get more information about this because I did not they anything about it. That is one of the motives that led me to go and see Mr. Karadzic. Another motive was that I should make the proposal that I already referred to, that Mr. Borovcanin should come with his unit. I noticed during this war, which was not a war between classical armies, it was the armed people that were waging war for the most part. I saw that some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. casualties were completely unnecessary and were due to the fact that these people were not well trained to conduct military operations. I must tell you that when I was touring the units this area, many of my colleagues, teachers, were at these positions, as well as managers from companies, people who were even elderly, who were unable, or at least that was my assessment, to make any major breakthroughs or take some fortified positions of the enemy, and so on and so forth. I understood at one point in time that the actions around Srebrenica were not only routine matters but that there was a serious objective involved to enter Srebrenica itself, and I understood that while I was in the field, and I thought that that would be disastrous for a great many people that I saw myself. Bratunac is a small town, we are all acquaintances and friends, and I thought that it would be a good thing that if the plans were the way they were, that a trained professional unit should come to the area. I knew Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin, I knew some people from his unit, and I thought that they were absolutely capable to carry out such a task. Of course it was for me to make a suggestion but it was up to the president to decide whether he would act in accordance with my suggestion or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. From what you say and from what you wrote in paragraph 171, it follows that you had actually noticed that apart from these Wolves from the Drina, it was ordinary men who were involved in combat, not trained soldiers, and that's why you suggested to Karadzic that the special unit of the MUP of Republika Srpska should be involved.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you now explained that in order to accomplish these missions which you knew nothing about, a unit like that was needed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I didn't say that I didn't know anything about it at that moment. I didn't know anything about the goals of the military operation in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica in the preceding period. At that time, I saw very intensive activity going on on the ground, and I saw that the move to take Srebrenica was impending. If I hadn't seen on the ground what I had seen, I wouldn't have gone to see President Karadzic. But since I witnessed the previous routine operations that took place, I could compare them to the current ones and see that it was not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood you as saying that you did not know the combat objectives of the units which were involved in those attacks and those operations around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, none of the people on the ground who were involved and who commanded these operations told me those goals word-for-word, but I was able, based on logic and experience, to make my own conclusions about the events I was witnessing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I received from my associates a couple of documents that I will try to clarify with your assistance. Are you aware that the corps commander, General Zivanovic, on the 2nd of July, 1995, issued an order to carry out active combat operations? That referred to the operation known as Krivaja 1995.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read out to you. It's dated 2nd of July, 1995, military secret, strictly confidential, copy number illegible, Krivaja 1995, order for active combat operations. There is reference to maps. On page 2, item 2, it says: "Command of the DK," meaning Drina Corps, "based on the instruction OP 71 of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska and based on the situation in the area of responsibility, has the order to carry out active combat operations, to separate the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica as soon as possible and reduce them to their urban areas." That's as far as I can see the objective. "Completely separate and reduce the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, improve the tactical position in-depth." That is the order of the commander. It is a pretty lengthy one. Order issued by Major General Zivanovic. You know this general, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this order, it is very clearly formulated what the objective is. The date is the 2nd of July. And then further on, I will quote from page 5 of this document. It reads: "Security organs and the military police will designate areas of assembly and the security of prisoners of war and war booty. In treatment of prisoners of war and the civilian population, adhere to the Geneva Conventions in full." That is what is written in the order of General Zivanovic regarding operations around Srebrenica. Are you saying, Mr. Deronjic, that you knew nothing about this, you as the person holding the highest responsibility for this area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But can we conclude from this order that already on the 2nd of July it was quite clear what the objectives of the operation were and how one should treat prisoners of war and the civilian population? It is written in this order and everyone who received this order behind the lines must have been aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say anything about this. I don't know who received the order. I didn't, and I don't see how I could be aware of it. But I do not dispute that the persons who did receive the order were well acquainted with its contents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would like to tender this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see it. Show it to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the witness may see it. This is a photocopy, and I don't have the original, but he will be able to see that it is an authentic order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I know you haven't seen this order, but perhaps you'd like just to have a look at it, and if you have any comment on it, to make it now. If not, we will simply take it, and we'll have a look up here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Excellency, it would take too much time for me to read all of this. I can only note that I'm seeing this for the first time. I had no prior occasion to see this document. If you want my comments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. What we'll do for the moment is perhaps we could have a look, and then I propose that we mark it for identification. Yes. We'll mark this for identification with the next D number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 219, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, Mr. Deronjic, did General Krstic, when you met him briefly at Pribicevac, him or some other qualified officer, did they tell you that the operation was not being implemented successfully?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember anything of the kind. At one point, I came to my own conclusion that it is not going on very successfully because I was present during an attempt of the Muslim forces within that protected area to push our forces back as far away from the focus of events as possible. But I didn't discuss it with General Krstic or any other officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, how did you then, as a layman, manage to notice that the operation is not going on very successfully and that it was necessary to engage this special unit, Special Police Unit of the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you don't seem to be listening to me. My motivation for the decision I made is varied. I am not a soldier, but I was able to see with my own eyes what was going on on the ground. A person who is able -- capable of logical thinking can make their own conclusions about whether a military operation is going on successfully or not. I was able to see that there were a lot of casualties, great losses Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were incurred, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Regardless of the fact that you haven't read that order, even I only glanced through it because my associates provided me with it only yesterday, I understood that the combat objectives of the Bratunac Brigade and the Milici Brigade where some display of force, in fact, that would tie up enemy forces and keep them engaged so that they would not be able to fight elsewhere. It was some sort of demonstrative action aimed at tying up enemy forces. That's what I understood from the documents available to me. That was the objective of the Bratunac and the Milici Brigades. Of course I don't have enough information to be certain about this.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you what I saw on the ground. The Bratunac Brigade for the most part was deployed in the area from Pribicevac to Bratunac. What its immediate objectives in the operation were, I really don't know, because it was only in the afternoon of the 11th that I met with the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, Mr. Blagojevic, and by then the order to go into Srebrenica had already been issued. The troops were already ordered to go in. I have no reason to doubt what you're saying, but I was simply not informed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 172, you say that you went to Pale to see Karadzic alone by night. What date was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I had to say that I could not say for certain. I told you it was a long time ago. I think it could have been either the 7th or the 8th or maybe the 9th. Most probably the 8th or the 9th. Those were the likely possible dates when I went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I had in mind that you went there on the 9th of July. Let me just look at this paragraph 172. It says: "I went to Pale alone on the 9th of July. Ljubisa Borovcanin came to Bratunac with his unit the next day." And then it goes on to say: "... so this is how I can determine the exact date of the visit." You seem to be pretty specific.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in my earlier statement I specified that it could have been the 8th or the 9th. You know, Mr. Milosevic, that I gave this statement without being able to refresh my memory, especially with regard to dates, because I was already in detention. So I expressed my reservation about the timing of certain events. And I didn't even think that I needed to be completely accurate. Unfortunately, I cannot tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let it be the 9th, as it says in your statement. Let us not go into that. These objectives of the operation -- and I suppose you know that I have been in detention for three years now, and it is very difficult for me to gain access to all sorts of documentation, but from what I do get to see, I can reconstruct certain events. So if you went on the 9th to ask what the objective was and the objectives are determined in the order dated the 2nd of July as separating Zepa, Srebrenica, taking hold of roads, et cetera - we can check all that - therefore, everybody involved in that operation in view of the order that had been issued must have been clear about the objectives. You, the top political chief in the area, are the only one who doesn't know the objectives so you have to go and see Karadzic on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know and I couldn't have known how long it was between the order and my visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm only pointing out the date of the order. And you went to see Karadzic seven days later. We're talking about an order that was widely known, that specified the objective of the operation. The fact that you went to see Karadzic seven days later is a bit unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point in arguing about this, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, the point is that it is my firm conviction that the statement of this witness in its main points is based on this plea agreement with the Prosecution, and these are contradictory matters, because if on the 2nd of July this order was issued in which the objectives are described --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's told you more than once, I don't know how many times he has to repeat it, he knows nothing about this order, nor do we. It's something that you've put up. Whether it was issued or not you can give evidence about, or whether anybody believed it you can give evidence about, whether it meant anything. But he doesn't know anything about it. That's his evidence. It's pointless to go on arguing and going over it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I care about having these things clarified. As you know full well, Serbia has nothing to do with this, but I do want to have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, since you went on the 9th or some day around the 9th of July to Pale, did you announce your arrival there? How could you know whether Karadzic was there, whether he was not there, especially in the evening, whether you could find him, whether he could receive you and so on? Did you telephone before that to make sure that he was there and that he could receive you? How did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I explained this. I explained it in my statement. Truth to tell, it's not contained in this particular version, but then as far as I know, you yourself visited Pale a few times. You know how big a place it is, and you know that Mr. Karadzic spent most of his time there. During the operations that had to do with Srebrenica, it was logical to assume that he would be at the Presidency or at one of the neighbouring buildings. My possibilities to get in touch with him were quite realistic. It was quite realistic for me to expect that I could find him in Pale and speak to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did visit in Pale once, and this was when the Assembly of Republika Srpska was meeting in relation to the Vance-Owen Plan. Yes, I do know that it is a small town and that before the war it was basically a tourist area. So you went, just like that, expecting to find him, and indeed you found him.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can put it that way. I did not want to make any assumptions here. I cannot remember whether I made a telephone call before that. That's why I didn't say anything. I could have stopped by the office and checked whether the president was in Pale, and that was sufficient. Then I could simply go to Pale and speak to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you then went to see him, did that have to be registered in some protocol book? Did this information have to be registered somewhere, when you visited him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any traces of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know about this, Mr. Milosevic. How could I know whether there was any trace of that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell anybody in Bratunac where you were going?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. Bratunac at that time was quite empty. Everybody was mobilised except for the staff in my office, and I'm primarily referring to my secretary. I said this to the Office of the Prosecutor. At that time, I was seeing Mr. Sinisa Glogovac at Pribicevac. He could have known. I'm not sure whether I told him, but I could have told him that I was going to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a second. I don't understand that. Now you're saying that you may have told Glogovac and before that you said that you had not told anyone.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, if you read this, I saw him at Pribicevac, and he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is he now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: He works at the state security of Republika Srpska, or rather, he was working there until the moment of my arrest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you went to Pale all by yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not tell anyone about this except that you may have told Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Sinisa Glogovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these claims of yours could perhaps only be supported by Glogovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's not true. It can be corroborated by Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Mr. Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And how far away is Bratunac from Pale? How much time was necessary in order to get there by car?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Bratunac is about 130 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: In my statement I said that I cannot remember the exact hour, but it could have been in the afternoon. Perhaps my memory can be playing tricks on me. This is in the mountains, and as you know, it gets dark there a bit earlier than in Bratunac, which is in a valley. But I think it was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that at the entrance into the Presidency building you saw Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Stanisic as they were walking about.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: As they were walking out of the Presidency building. I didn't see them as they actually walked out, I just saw encountered them there. I could explain the Presidency building in detail and the place where I saw them. This was on the left hand of the Presidency building. They were getting out of the Presidency building, and they were getting closer to the exit from the yard of the Presidency building, and that's where I encountered them. I'm not saying that they were taking a walk in that sense, I mean that they were strolling in the street or something like that. They were simply walking at a slow pace, and they were talking amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 173, you say that knowing the position Jovica Stanisic held, you assumed that they were talking about Srebrenica. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that on that occasion, Radovan Karadzic introduced you to Jovica Stanisic, and he said, "This is one of our guys from the area." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that why you concluded that they were talking about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, that among other things, but also his very presence there at Pale at the moment when this military operation is taking place, a military operation that is of significance. And I assume that his presence at Pale at that moment had to do with the operations around Srebrenica. I'm not asserting that. I did not have any facts at my disposal to be able to say this for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This expression that someone is from down there, from the field, in the communications that I know of, this usually has to do with local leaders from the field, from the area.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have to add something, Mr. Milosevic. When it's -- when somebody says, "This is a guy of ours from there, from the field, from the area."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: But if this has to do with an event that is about to take place or that is taking place when it just says "down there" without saying Bratunac, Trebinje, Zvornik, Bijeljina, et cetera, then it means that this from "down there" is something that people know of on the basis of something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only thing that was going on at the time, or was this a general way of putting things when people were being introduced, saying that somebody was a local leader?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what Mr. Karadzic said, the way he had phrased it, and on the basis of the fact that right afterwards we talked about the events in Srebrenica, I drew the only logical conclusion, that the conversation that they were having had to do with Srebrenica too. And I'm not even claiming that, I said that I assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know why and on the basis of what you could make such an assumption except for what you say just now and which is very flimsy grounds for this kind of assumption. Please tell me, Mr. Deronjic, why do you think they were discussing Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, I believe that the Trial Chamber has understood what I've been saying. I used -- I said that the president used a general term, "from down there." It meant that it would be known where I was coming from exactly, and that is something that addresses your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then he took you to the side; is that right? And while Krajisnik and Stanisic waited a few steps away from you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not waiting, they were talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. They were standing there talking between themselves, and he took you to the side a few steps from them.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you talked about this engagement of Borovcanin; is that right? That was a proposal made and he said that that proposal would be carried through; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or rather, he said that it was a good proposal but that it was impossible to be carried through because he was engaged in the Sarajevo theatre of war near Kalinovik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what he said. He agreed to my proposal, he agreed with my proposal, and it was my impression that he would it carried through, which ultimately did take place, but he said that he certainly had to discuss this with the minister of the interior, because that unit was indeed engaged in the area around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say Karadzic apologised to Krajisnik and Stanisic - that is 176 - "and took me to the side, to the left, some five or six steps from them. I then asked him what the exact goal was for the operation in Srebrenica." That is when you asked him what was the exact goal for the operation in Srebrenica. You did not know anything in relation to these orders and things like that. And then Karadzic said to you that there are two plans concerning the Srebrenica option or options that had been agreed to. Plan option A is liberation of the road on the south side and a reduction of the protected zone, safe haven of Srebrenica to the size that had been agreed to or described in UN documents. Plan/option B -- I mean I'm reading paragraph 177. Plan/option B was entering Srebrenica and taking it militarily. He made it known that option B or plan B was a tentative one, a conditional, and that it would only come into effect if it was militarily doable, practical. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me just go through this now because your statement is very long, many pages. Now, you say: "The second issue was actually my proposal, that if they do not want to enter Srebrenica, then it would be indispensable to bring a serious military unit to that area. I told Karadzic quite openly that I trusted Ljubisa Borovcanin's military skills and his personal qualities. Karadzic agreed in principle but quickly explained that the unit was engaged in the Sarajevo area in Kalinovik. I was persistent and had the impression that my request would be granted." So that's what happened then when you talked about it. And you say that practically Borovcanin came the day after you had been in Pale. That's what you said in the paragraph that I quoted to you a few minutes ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. That is what I said, but I keep telling you time and again that I'm not sure about all these dates. I told you that just a day or two after that Ljubisa Borovcanin came to Bratunac. It is very hard for me to remember each and every date exactly now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you this without any intention of leading you to any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. kind of contradiction. I'm simply going through your statement. You said that on the following day, he came to Bratunac with his unit. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, what I learned subsequently, the information I obtained subsequently over here, Ljubisa came to Bratunac on the 10th or 11th. So up to a degree what I said is contradictory, but I told the Office of the Prosecutor quite clearly that I'm not certain of each and every date regarding these events, because I did not take part in some of them directly. I did not meet Ljubisa there in Bratunac when we came there, so I just gave my opinion as to when he could have come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Deronjic. Now, in paragraph 180, you say: "Karadzic asked me, 'What do you, Miroslav, intend to do with that population down there?' I perhaps did not quote him exactly, but I remember clearly him using the word 'you,' meaning in plural. As far as I know, he used the second person plural when addressing practically everyone as a matter of courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he addressed you in such terms as well; is that right?. Did he speak to you addressing you in the second person singular, saying "ti"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you this. So he addressed you in the second person plural as well, as a matter of courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you cannot be quite certain that when he said "vi" in the sense of the second person plural, it wasn't really in the plural but he was addressing you personally as an act of courtesy as an official he was speaking to.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President -- Mr. Milosevic, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Perhaps I misspoke. I said "Mr. President" and you're not the president now and I had no intention of saying that actually. But you forget the fact, and perhaps you don't even know it, I am a language teacher. I can feel this finesse, nuance in expression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste any time over that. In communications --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us adjourn now because we're past the time. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go on, Mr. Milosevic, until 2.00 to try and make up some of the time that's been lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in paragraph 181, you claim that Karadzic at one point told you, "Miroslav, all of them need to be killed." And then you say that you are 100 per cent sure that he used those precise words. Is that right, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. It's true that he uttered that sentence, but I added, and I would kindly ask you to read the entire context, that he said a couple of more things. And I said in reference to the last thing he said, namely the principles of Western Slavonia, that I'm 100 per cent sure that he used those words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you're not 100 per cent sure that he said all of them need to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that he said it. I'm not sure of the precise words, but the gist of what he said was that all of those people needed to be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All this is going on on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, provided that I was there on the 9th; and I expressed my reservations about the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that coincided with the arrival of Borovcanin, which was on the 10th or 11th. So you were there on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It could have been the 7th or the 8th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that Srebrenica hadn't been taken yet.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, it hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is that supposed to mean, that they all need to be killed if Srebrenica hadn't been taken yet?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, Karadzic previously told me that our forces would go into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back later to that when we have more elements and clarify it, I hope. But now I want to ask you this: At that time, and generally speaking, Mr. Deronjic, did you have any role in the command chain, in the chain of command of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I had no role whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any way you could have affected the decisions of commanders in the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You couldn't. How, then, do you explain the fact that Radovan Karadzic told you that all of them needed to be killed if you were not able to do that, according to your own words?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he couldn't have issued that order to you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It was not an order that he issued to me. At the time when we were speaking, it was clear to me and clear to him that it was not an order. It was a possible outcome of the events in Srebrenica. Let me just add that we discussed Srebrenica more than once and that at our various meetings, we discussed the possible amount of population in Srebrenica. And the question that imposed itself was what would happen when our troops entered Srebrenica to the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Radovan Karadzic only on the 9th of July, in the evening, when you claim you were with him, learnt from talking on the phone to General Tolimir that there was a chance of capturing Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't know that, do you know that it was from that information that the order of Karadzic followed to Generals Gvero and Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I heard about that from one testimony in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is an order issued on the 9th of July, 1995, signed by General Tolimir, where it says, among other things: "In keeping with the orders of the president of the republic, the order is issued to all units involved in military combat activities around Srebrenica to ensure maximum protection and safety to UNPROFOR troops and the civilian population. Forward this order to all units to refrain from destroying any civilian facilities unless forced to defend themselves. Refrain from destroying property and treat prisoners of war and the civilian population in keeping with the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949." I am quoting from an order which I have in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that order in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't see that order before, and you didn't know about it at the time of the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. I never even saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is clear that what is conveyed here is the order from President Karadzic himself on how to treat civilians and prisoners of war, and it says that this order needs to be forwarded to all commanders in all units involved.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is dated 9th of July, 1995. Is it then clear, Mr. Deronjic, that on the 9th of July, on that day you had no direct or telephone contact with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, you cannot draw the conclusion that I was not at Pale then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that conclusion cannot be drawn, then can we conclude that it is indisputable in view of this order that Karadzic could not have issued the order to kill people either to you or to anyone else? That's precisely what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I told you, Mr. Milosevic, what we discussed. I never said that it was in the form of order either to me or addressed to anyone else. It was a conversation that followed after I learned that troops would enter Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srebrenica. The president wanted to explain to me in a few words what could be the epilogue and the denouement of these developments. He referred to the principles of Western Slavonia. You do not believe, I hope, that I imagined in some magic way this particular phrasing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't imagine anything. I'm presenting to you a document which speaks clearly that Karadzic could not have told you or anyone else that people needed to be killed. His orders are quite to the contrary: Take care of the prisoners of war, civilians, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You have not paid attention to the witness's answer, and you must do that if you are to cross-examine him properly. You keep insisting that Karadzic was issuing an order, he tells you plainly, the witness, that it was no order, it was simply a comment which Karadzic made. There's no good repeating that it was an order when the witness says firmly it wasn't. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the point here is not whether it was the order. The point is that what I just quoted was an order, and the order clearly shows that Karadzic is saying that prisoners of war, civilians, and the UNPROFOR troops should be treated in keeping with the Geneva Conventions. That is why I am disputing that Karadzic could have said to anyone, to this witness or anyone else, that people needed to be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said to you quite plainly that that is what Karadzic said to him. Whatever other documents he may have issued, whether they were truthful ones or not, doesn't matter. It's the witness's evidence which we are dealing with at the moment. You can produce other evidence in due course if you want, but you have heard what this witness says; Karadzic told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, to assist, the document that the accused is referring to is, I think, already in as D171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Marked for identification, I understand, at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the document that's just been handed to you I think is the document that the accused had marked for identification earlier. It comes from our collection. You now have an English version of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have now got 171 too. Yes, we've got this order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. It's not necessary for me to tender it again, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to tender it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Deronjic. When you referred to this principle of Western Slavonia, which is something that Karadzic referred to himself in this conversation with you, there were only the two of you present then; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the moment when he referred to Western Slavonia and he said all these things, we were standing about five or six steps away from Momcilo Krajisnik and Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You explained that they were talking between the two of them and he took you aside to talk to you separately; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when up mentioned this principle of Western Slavonia, do you know that during the events that took place in the Operation Flash, there occurred a mass expulsion of Serbs from that territory? That was the context. It could not have meant kill them all. How did you deduce that it meant kill them all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, never did I say that I inferred that they all needed to be killed. I quoted, memory permitting, what I remember from that conversation, and my comment which I stated in my statement was that I replied there was no way I could forecast what would happen on the ground. That is one. Second, the events in Western Slavonia that occurred on the 1st of May, if I'm not mistaken, were commented upon by the leadership, the Serb leadership of Republika Srpska, and the media. It was accepted wisdom at the time that the Croatian army attacked not only the fleeing troops but the civilians who were fleeing together with the troops. I think it was widely reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The events from Western Slavonia are well known, but it could not have meant for a second that all of them needed to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: There is a continuation to this sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that Vidoje Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade, ordered to you to go into Srebrenica - that is in paragraph 184 - on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you found out on your way to Srebrenica that Karadzic was looking for you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why you didn't go into Srebrenica. You returned to Bratunac instead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Couldn't you have talked to Karadzic from Srebrenica? Did you have to return to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't because the troops had not yet entered Srebrenica. They were just moving towards it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So when you established contact with him - I'm drawing your attention to paragraph 185 - the first thing he asked was the following: "Deronjic, is my information correct that we had entered Srebrenica?"

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, then, how do you explain the discrepancy in what you are saying? Radovan Karadzic, president of the Republika Srpska and its Supreme Commander, the Supreme Commander of its army, who only a day before, in your own words, spoke to you about plans A and B and told you to kill everyone, did not know how the Srebrenica operation was proceeding and that he did not know whether his own troops had entered the town and had instead to ask you. How come he was calling precisely you, of all people, to ask this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, first of all, I want to say that these quotation marks you see sometimes in my statement are not necessarily correctly placed, because when my testimony was summarised, certain things may have been marked as a quotation incorrectly. Second, as I said, he was just asking me to confirm the information he had already received. What is illogical about that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He asked, "Is my information correct?"

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it means he already was in possession of that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was asking you whether it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that telephone conversation, among other things, Karadzic explained to you what your duties would be as the newly-appointed commissioner for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me briefly, what did he say about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: The gist of his instructions to me had to do with the fate of the civilians who were gathering in Potocari as we were speaking. He told me to propose to them three alternatives and to establish contact with Mladic, if possible. If you want me, I can describe to you the three alternatives that I was supposed to convey to Muslim representatives regarding their own treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But the first alternative, the first option was to tell them that they could stay in Srebrenica. Everybody who wanted to stay in Srebrenica could do so.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say in your statement that it was complete madness. This idea was complete madness.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. If you want me to put it this way, it was mission impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to me the following: When he told you to tell the Muslims that everybody who wanted to stay in Srebrenica could, why was that madness?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I have already given you five or six reasons for that, and I can repeat them if necessary. I don't think it is necessary. I think all those reasons were widely known to Mr. Karadzic, to myself, and everybody involved. You cannot seriously contend that that population, those people, could have stayed in Srebrenica unhindered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I know is that all the decisions and conclusions of the leadership was that the population should be allowed to stay where they were, not only in Srebrenica but in all other areas.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know about any conclusions of the kind. Developments in the field spoke to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: I have this document that I had been served with related to another witness. It says that the leadership of the SDS issued instructions on the organisation and activity of the Serb population in a state of emergency, and in item 8, because these are the instructions you followed, reads: "In undertaking all these measures, make sure that ethnic civil and other rights of all ethnicities are observed and that they are organised under the conclusions of the Serb authorities in the given municipality." So that was a general conclusion, that ethnic and other rights of all peoples should be respected and that they should be represented in government bodies to be established later.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since Mr. Nice insisted that there were Variants A and B according to which members of other ethnicities from those areas should be removed, and I did not find it anywhere in the programme of the SDS; on the contrary, I see they speak of respecting the rights of all peoples.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: It's true that it doesn't say so in the instructions, and I never claimed that the document titled Variant A and B was the only reason that caused a great number of people from that area to flee. It was just an element, as I said, in the entire plan which caused the expulsion and fleeing of those people. The events from the end of the war - let me add this - have very little in common with the situation from the beginning of the war. There were -- in the situation in Srebrenica as it was in 1995, with Serbs ruling, it was absolutely impossible for the Muslims to stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That may be your judgement, shared by other people perhaps, but what I quoted was a generally accepted political stance expressed here. But let us come back to the fact that you were the newly-appointed civilian commissioner for Srebrenica. You discussed those two variants. Is it true that he told you that you needed to contact General Mladic, speaking of those three options, because General Mladic was in charge, and you needed to agree on a meeting with the UNPROFOR and with the Muslims to discuss these three options? I'm speaking about paragraph 187.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I will have to answer something else, to address something else that you alluded to when you just spoke now. I'm going to remind you that in 1992, an enormous number of Muslims from the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I'm talking about Muslims, left the area, including leave the municipality of Bratunac and Zvornik. If those were not the intention of the leaders of Republika Srpska, do we know that somebody was arrested, tried because of this, or convicted?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I could address that question to you because you were an official of Republika Srpska, not me. You were an official of the SDS, not I.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
