utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm telling you, Mr. Milosevic, because I know this, and I assume that I know it better than you do. Nobody was punished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume -- well, it's not that I assume, I know for sure that you know this better than I do. All right now.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Shall we go back to this question, if you wish, the one related to Mladic, the one that you put to me just now? I said that he had said to me that Mr. Karadzic had told me to contact Mr. Mladic about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and then you presented these options there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: At the meeting on the 12th of July at the Fontana Hotel, I presented these options.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the first option was that the Muslims should stay in Srebrenica, those who wished to do so; and the second option was that they should go where the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in control, in the direction of Kladanj; and the third was to go wherever they wished to go, some third countries. So theoretically these were the only three options; for them to stay, to go to territories that were under their control, or to go to other places as refugees, wherever they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you say that Karadzic on that occasion warned that it's possible that some war criminals might try to hide among the civilians and that he insisted that such people, if found, should be kept behind or held, because you had the right to do that in accordance with the conventions that had to do with the customs of war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he only wanted war criminals to be detained if such people were to be found, and also the conventions that relate to customs of war should be abided by.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Radovan Karadzic, this same person who is telling you that everybody should be killed, all the Muslims in Srebrenica, later on insists that you meet in your capacity as new civilian commissioner with the Muslims, with Mladic and UNPROFOR, that you present these three options. That you present these three options and also you try to identify war criminals in the ranks of the Muslims. Mr. Deronjic, isn't that quite contradictory in relation to what you asserted before, that he had said to you that all the Muslims should be killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. To a degree, these orders that I had received directly over the telephone are contradictory to what the president told me on the 9th of July, but let me explain. Let's dispel any possible doubt. Do you think that in public directly he would tell me of any other intentions that possibly - and I'm not claiming anything - he or somebody else might have had and that these intentions could be carried through in Potocari with the presence of the international forces, notably UNPROFOR? And some journalists had already arrived as well. I'm not speculating on this but I don't want to owe you any answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, precisely. I don't think that anyone should speculate because the entire idea is sheer madness, to have all these people killed. Isn't that clear to everyone who has any degree of common sense? That's why I find this incredible, that you say to me, "Karadzic told me, kill everyone."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you keep repeating time and again only part of my statement. When you put it that way, "kill everyone," it can imply exactly what I've been saying, but he added yet another sentence, "everything you can." So when he says "everything you can," then he's not referring to absolutely everything, everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, whatever you managed to, in that sense. But it is sheer madness for anyone to present that kind of idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You know, we have been over this for half an hour. You've been wasting time going over the same point. The witness has given his evidence. This is what he claims Karadzic said. That's his evidence, that that is what Karadzic said. There's no point going over it and saying you found it contrary to common sense and whatever else. The point is the witness's evidence is to that effect. Your going on asking him the same question doesn't help. Now, if you want more time and you're asking for it, you must use your time usefully and not repeating.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm not putting same question to him all the time, Mr. May, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Deronjic, is it also correct that on that occasion he say to you on that it was necessary for you yourself to enter Srebrenica and to establish the police there to secure facilities and to establish control over town?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Once the conditions are right for me to enter Srebrenica, that was one of the primary tasks that I was given that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you got -- and you asked him to give you all these orders in writing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I asked to get an order on my appointment because it would have been wrong for me to do anything or say anything without that kind of order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in relation to this establishment of the police, securing facilities, establishing control over town generally speaking, protection and so on, this was your task as civilian commissioner; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You asked for him to give it to you in writing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then if you asked for all of this, how come you didn't ask for the order to have someone killed when that is a cardinal thing? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Milosevic, we're going back to the same thing yet again. I never said that everybody should be killed. You keep neglecting all the time that I explained what "everybody" meant. The principle of Western Slavonia, the army fleeing in different directions, possibly civilians too, and that these columns should then be targeted. That is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that that evening on the 11th you found out from people in the area, as you claimed, that a large number of military-age Muslims withdrew in the direction of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the numbers involved and how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I presented my opinion on this. I gave President Karadzic my opinion too, that it was 15 to 20.000 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many of them were armed. Many of these people managed to get through to Tuzla having used weapons. I cannot give this evidence. It's not possible for me to know this. But I assume that an enormous number of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So then, being armed and through fighting, they worked their way all the way through to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, a part of them were armed, but I don't know how many actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Next morning early, on the 12th, you were told that Mladic was looking for you and that he was waiting to see you at a meeting at the Fontana Hotel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the meeting was attended by Muslim representatives and you recognised two of them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that at this meeting they kept insisting that they wanted to leave Srebrenica safely?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nevertheless you presented the three options to them, the ones that Karadzic told you about the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also to detain persons for which civilian and military authorities ascertained that they had something to do with the commission of crimes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I thought that you could not remember and I wanted to remind you. That is paragraph 193.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, sorry. We had to pause between question and answer and you weren't finishing so I was waiting for you to finish your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But in spite of that, the Muslim representatives insisted that the Muslims leave Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it beyond any doubt, Mr. Deronjic, in view of this insistence on the offered options, that the Srebrenica Muslims and all the others who were in the safe haven left Srebrenica at their own insistence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That is a fact that is beyond any doubt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were not expelled. They left Srebrenica at their own insistence.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Due to all these activities. I think that there was no other solution anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct, Mr. Deronjic, that Karadzic telephoned you the following day as well, on the 13th of July, to find out how the transport of civilians was progressing and to express his interest in the fighting that took place the previous day, on the 12th, in the area of Konjevic Polje. This is paragraph 199 through 201.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you said to him then that over a half of the civilians had been transported by the time he made his telephone call and that in the area of Konjevic Polje 12 to 15.000 people were pushing through in the direction of Tuzla with heavy fighting and that you could even hear fire exchanges and even artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if each and every word is correct, but that is the essence of my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then you did not tell Karadzic on that occasion that in the area of Konjevic Polje that they were already capturing or arresting Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. I did not tell him that because this is a telephone call from my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you keep silent about that when speaking to him? Don't you think that if you told him about it then that he could have stopped such activities such as killings by way of his authority?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, during a previous meeting I had, and that was on the 11th, I was warned that if I had some information that I should go through military channels. Also, anything that could be dangerous -- I mean, that meant anything that could have been dangerous because of eavesdropping. And also I was invited precisely because of this meeting to come to Pale. So I had the possibility on the 14th in the morning to inform the president about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That means that until then he could not have been informed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said. On the contrary. There are three possibilities to inform the president from that area. One is the military line, the Ministry of the Interior, the head of the public security station, Mr. Vasic, and the state security with the office in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 201, since you talk about liquidations, in some way you are trying to say, and I want to be quite precise, when I say "liquidations," I mean killings. I mean somebody was killed. It doesn't have to mean that a person was executed, it means that these persons were killed, lost their lives. What does this mean, not shot but liquidated, executed? Isn't that one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: How could it be one and the same thing, Mr. Milosevic? Somebody could be taken prisoner and then shot, and then also a person could get killed in fighting during a breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What is your knowledge? How many of them were killed during this fighting, during the breakthrough that we referred to a few minutes ago when you said 12 to 15.000 persons were pushing their -- were trying to get to Tuzla with heavy fighting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I'm try to explain, Mr. Milosevic. We did not have any information at the time. I had semi-information, information from people in the field involving primarily the police high officials who were involved in these communications. They told me that there were killings and that there were liquidations. That meant that fighting had already been going on, and of course there were casualties in fighting, in combat. But also, people were being taken prisoner and liquidated, as they told me. The information I got about these events subsequently, that is to say not on that day but later, much later, I found out that there were very many people in that region who were killed in combat. I even had the opportunity of informing the international public about this. When Mrs. Elizabeth Wren visited Bratunac, I told them that in that area there were a great many people who had been killed. They visited the area. I don't know what the figures involved were, but very many people were killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just explain one thing to me, please -- rather, what was your information on that day? Liquidations of prisoners on that day or were most of the casualties due to the combat that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I had both pieces of information on that day, namely that there were casualties as a result of combat but also that there were persons who were taken prisoner and killed. Revenge was also mentioned, that people were doing this at their own initiative. That was the information I received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have, or rather, did you have on that day any information as to the scope of the killings? I'm not talking about combat casualties. You said that many people were killed in combat. Were these individual cases of revenge and similar matters, as you said just now, or did you have information that many people were killed that way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, in the afternoon -- that is to say in the evening, rather, but not at the moment when I spoke to Karadzic on the telephone when he called me. So on the 13th, in the afternoon and in the evening, I had received information that at the Kravica cooperative, several persons had been killed. I don't know who conveyed this information to me, but it was explained to me by Mr. Borovcanin in the evening, namely what had happened exactly. That involves a great many victims. That is my answer to your question. Everything else that I heard, that I mentioned can refer to individual cases but I do not have much information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on that day when you talked to Karadzic, you had not received information about this yet, what you said just now at the cooperative, at the farm, that there had been many persons who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then after that did you inform Karadzic about this or anybody else from the leadership, either civilian or military leadership, about what had happened, what you found out later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you inform him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: On the 14th. Because on the 13th I was invited to come to Pale. So on the morning of the 14th, sometime during the morning, I was in Pale and I said this to the president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we get to the 14th when you were in Pale, the person who informed you about this, what had happened, did this person tell you who had committed the killings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, this was not something he said to me. This person told me the circumstances under which these persons were killed at the cooperative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand what "circumstances" means. He did not tell you who killed these people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Of course not. I don't think he knew at that moment. This was right after that. How could he have known? How could he investigate so quickly and tell me about this? He told me that these were the units that happened to be there, including his own unit of the special police. But I do not preclude the possibility of somebody else having taken place in that, even until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 205 you say that Borovcanin said to you that Mladic had issued orders for the army to move to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: You mean 205, paragraph 205?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that this information was something you found upsetting because, as you say, the majority of the Muslim forces were not defeated and were very close to Bratunac, to the Bratunac area.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in spite of the fact that the majority of the Muslim forces had not been defeated yet, Mladic, with the bulk of his forces, moves towards Zepa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: He issues orders for the army to go to Zepa, and I do not know how many forces actually went to Zepa and how this evolved in formal terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, then, Mr. Deronjic, does it mean that already on the 13th and the 14th Mladic was not in Srebrenica any more?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: How could I draw that conclusion? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were informed that Mladic had moved on towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. Borovcanin said that an order had been issued for troops to move on. First of all, the troops did not necessarily move on that very day; and second, Borovcanin did not necessarily have to go with then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 206, you say that due to the great number of captured Muslims who were in danger of being killed, you called Karadzic to ask him what to do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you by that time have very clear instructions from both Karadzic and Tolimir that all civilians, all Muslims should be given security and treated in keeping with Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: How could I have had this information? I told you I did not know about that order that you mentioned. Second, even if I had known about it, at that moment the prisoners were not guarded properly, were not kept in appropriate premises and killings were already taking place in the Vuk Karadzic school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that Karadzic told you on that occasion, "Well, Miroslav, can you hear me? I'm going to send such-and-such a man who will be carrying instructions."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the kind of conversation you have with mediators, with go-betweens involved?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This conversation was first transcribed in hand and then typed out. I don't know what "B" means and "D." "D" must be for Deronjic, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And "B" is the go-between. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm not disputing any of these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, then, where does this transcript come from? What is true about this? What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I told you. It was my conversation with President Karadzic, and I'm not going to go into whether it was recorded or intercepted. That's what we talked about on the phone. And I told you that I described this conversation even before I found out that this transcript existed, and I can confirm every sentence here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But until I saw this transcript, which was very recently, it seems that you were not talking to Karadzic. You were talking to a mediator.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I talked and explained to the Office of the Prosecutor. At one point I heard the voice of President Karadzic, but I'm not going to claim that any of these sentences were uttered by him. Many of them were conveyed by a go-between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point you say: "Can we hear each other, President?" And the go-between says: "The president cannot hear you. This is the intermediary." And then you go on to say: "I have about 2.000 here now by --" and in brackets it says the teleprinter drowns him out. I suppose that it was some sort of background hum. And then the president says: "All the goods must be placed in warehouses before 12.00 tomorrow," and you reply: "Right." And then this "X" says: "Deronjic, not in the warehouses but somewhere else." Could you please explain which part of this is something that he said, and what did you mean in the last line by "understood"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Milosevic, this is not a complete recording of my conversation with President Karadzic. That conversation included other things as well. You have three dots here after the word "by". It means that there were interruptions in that conversation, or at least in the record. I pointed this out to the Office of the Prosecutor, and they confirmed it. Second, a part of the conversation was indeed drowned out by a teleprinter. Third, I asked for instructions as to how to treat the captured Muslims. Instructions not for myself. My primary intention was to inform the president very briefly, because I could not give him all the details over the phone, I just told him the number of prisoners in Bratunac and asked how to treat them. And to that Karadzic or the mediator, whoever, said that they should be placed in warehouses but not in Bratunac but elsewhere, from which I understood that they should not be held in Bratunac. That was something I thought even before the conversation, and I just understood him as confirming my own idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you about this part. You say at this point that they should not stay in Bratunac but they should be evacuated instead.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no mention of liquidation at all.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, not in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reference is made to evacuation from Bratunac. Is it possible then, since you stated earlier, I don't know in which paragraph but when you described your duties as civilian commissioner to provide material supplies or war booty, could "goods" here be a reference to war booty?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Mr. Milosevic. I relayed to the president information that I couldn't go in detail on the phone, and I told him about how many people were captured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that number 2.000?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. He asked me, and I gave him my rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is this mediator to whom you spoke? Do you have any information at all about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I have no precise information, and my memory of these events has faded considerably. But that was a military communication line from the Bratunac Brigade with the president. I don't know how it works, technically speaking. All I know is that somebody would say, "Hello. You are now talking to the president. You can start talking," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So indeed if this is a reference to people, the order is to evacuate them from Bratunac, not to liquidate them.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He says that they should be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you say you wanted to inform him that people had been killed in the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: My intention when I went to speak to Karadzic was to warn him that there were incidents and killings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was your intention but you didn't actually inform him.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I believe I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Because it is not the best idea to say such things on the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You implied, you thought, that he needed to be informed, as you just said, because something needed to be done to prevent this.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Milosevic. I cannot remember the exact words in that conversation, but I did use hints and allusions to relay the most important information, and I think he understood me well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was talking to you, and you informed him as the main person, the civilian commissioner for Srebrenica, that killings were occurring, and you didn't know at the time on what kind of scale it was going on. But I suppose that at the moment you did intend to put a stop to it, to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. And that was one of my intentions when I went to have this conversation. I will not mention all the other measures I took. If the Court asks me, I will describe them. You mention that I was appointed civilian commissioner for the area of Srebrenica with a very strictly defined purview. If you think that these killings were also part of my responsibility, I reacted to them as a human being. It had nothing to do with my duties, with my official responsibilities. I want to remind you that the complete staff of the army of Republika Srpska was present there. Everyone from the Main Staff to brigade staffs, all the relevant steps in the hierarchy were represented, including the police force, and with all that in mind, do you really think it was my job to secure those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that if you are Man Number One in political and administrative terms, it is your job to protect these people, or at least to protect them from these killings. And what have you done about it? You didn't even inform Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Interpreters are warning me to make pauses. It is absolutely true that I did take certain actions. In my statement, I enumerated them. I invited police officers to come to my office. I asked them to provide better protection to those prisoners. During the night, certain people, retired people and even underage people, were mobilised and engaged as security. Bratunac was absolutely empty at that time. All available forces were engaged along the axes of combat that were exactly 22 kilometres away from Bratunac. I did inform the president, using indirect speech, telling him that bad things were happening, and he understood me very well. I apologise to the interpreters. I told him that this transcript is not a reflection of the entirety of my conversation. You can ask for an expertise and you will see that there were other things said during that conversation. Wait. Don't interrupt me. I haven't finished answering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to tell you that I cannot consult documents that have never been given to me. I don't want to put you on an unequal footing in this discussion. This is an exhibit of the side opposite, and if there are any inconsistencies, I want you to point them out.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I will. That's precisely why I'm saying this. Let me give you a comparison. In 1992, when volunteers came, 32 of them, armed to their teeth, started killings in Bratunac. At that time, I am a civilian, a political figure. How do you think that I could have adequately protected those people in Bratunac on the 13th of July, 1995, if I was unable to act in 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said yourself that you didn't even inform Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I informed Mr. Karadzic of that on the 14th in the morning, because after the conversation we had in the afternoon on the 13th, I knew that I would meet him at Pale the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we move on to the 14th, you say that on the 13th in the evening, a colonel or a lieutenant colonel burst into your office. Some sort of intelligence officer or security officer of the army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Colonel Beara -- and you supposed, you assumed that he was an emissary from Karadzic conveying his orders.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you assume that? On what basis? Did he say in so many words that he was coming on behalf of the president of the republic or was it as you say, that he barged in, he was in his cups. Did he say that he was coming with a message from the president of the republic, Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I will answer your questions one by one. Your first question was how could I have known that he was coming from Karadzic. I just explained to you that I had talked to Karadzic three or four hours prior to that, and he told me, without naming names, that a man would come - I explained this in precise terms to the Office of the Prosecutor - a man come carrying instructions. The arrival of Beara even took me by surprise. I didn't know. I didn't expect that he would come to my office. I was concerned about the situation in Bratunac, and I was looking for a way out, for a solution. It is true that Beara did not say in so many words that he was coming with instructions from President Karadzic. It is my inference that he was coming with instructions, and it is based on the fact that he later took charge of these people and the security provided to them, and on the fact that nobody else appeared in Bratunac after that with any sort of instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me, what exactly did Beara tell you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to explicit orders, he told me, "Mr. Deronjic, I have orders from the top that these people should be killed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He told you he had orders that these people should be killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you inferred it was coming from Karadzic, although he didn't tell you so.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: At that moment, I was not thinking about that. He just said from the top, from above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From above. And you asked Ljubo Simic -- who is Ljubo Simic, tell me.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: The president of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you asked this Ljubo Simic to leave you alone in the office because you wanted to be one-on-one with Beara.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you remained one-on-one, wasn't it natural to ask him, "Did Karadzic send you? Who gave you these orders?" Once you had removed this person who was your Man Number Two, a municipal official, wasn't it logical to ask the question, "Who sent you, and what exactly did they say?"

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I talked to Beara for a couple of minutes, maybe 10. He spent some time, quite some time in my office, because he was inebriated, as I explained to the Office of the Prosecutor, and this is just an expert -- excerpt from my description. And I quoted only the most relevant facts that he stated. I returned to my office after seeing Mr. Simic off, and then speaking in a rather sharp tone, I told Beara, "What you are conveying to me as orders does not coincide with the instructions I received from President Karadzic." And then we had a confrontation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to you, Beara told you that people needed to be killed, people should be killed, and you replied that that was not in accordance with Karadzic's instructions. And an hour or two ago you explained that it was Karadzic who told you that people should be killed, everyone should be killed. Is it now clear that Karadzic did not tell you that everyone needed to be killed, and it is questionable even what Beara told you if he was so drunk as you say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going over that point yet again. We've been over it I think 20 times. No need to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, what Beara allegedly said, did he say it in front of Simic or did he say it after you had removed Simic from the office?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: The direct order, the way he conveyed it to me is what he said after Mr. Simic left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Simic cannot corroborate what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Not this order. Not for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to what your statement says, after you sent Simic away, you told Beara that you had talked to Karadzic and that the prisoners should be taken out of Bratunac, evacuated from Bratunac, that is, towards Bijeljina, Batkovic. Well, Batkovic was a kind of collection centre, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what it was, but I had information that it was a prison, a military prison in the area around Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you conveyed to him that in agreement with Karadzic, these prisoners should be taken to the military prison?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was in accordance with the instructions you had received from Karadzic when he had said to you that the prisoners should be taken to the military prison in order to establish whether there were any war criminals among them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you quite precisely that was my interpretation of the president's instructions and I acted in accordance with my own interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your interpretation of his instructions was that the prisoners or, rather, prisoners of war should be taken to the military prison.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not killed; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the basis of what you said, that Karadzic said that a man would come who would tell you what to do, not to hand over the prisoners to him or anything else; is that right? He said a man would come who would tell you what to do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. He did not say that a man would come who would tell me that, and I do not have any kind of direct role. It's not that I am supposed to hand over the prisoners to anyone. My concern had to do with the fact the president said, "All right. I'll send a man who has instructions." So what did I have to do with that? I mean, how could I hand over anyone to the military? How could I hand over the military prisoners to the military itself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was wondering too.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No. That's not what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in accordance with Karadzic's instructions, you insist that they be evacuated to the military prison, these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I insisted they be taken there because that was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that was your understanding of what Karadzic said, that he asked for the prisoners to be sent to the military prison.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after this meeting with Beara -- and he had not been announced to you because you say that he just barged into your office.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this meeting ended in the early morning hours on the 14th of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You informed Karadzic and you asked him whether that was the man who was allegedly supposed to convey instructions, is that right, since you did not ask this man?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I did not because this was late in the night or, rather, already the morning of the 14th of July, and that morning I went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Before you went to Pale, you say in paragraph 211 that you met up with Beara again that morning, that is to say the 14th of July, halfway in relation to a place that you marked here as the brick factory and Bratunac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: In the morning of the 14th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when? You say that you ended that meeting in the morning. So again you say "in the morning." What does this term "in the morning" actually mean? When did you meet Beara on this road leading to the brick factory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Lest there be any conclusion so that you would not confuse anyone else or that you would not be confused, this meeting took place in my office with Beara during the night until the early morning hours, and it can be concluded, since I say "in the night," that it had not dawned yet. After that meeting, I went home. I decided to get some rest, to get a bit of sleep for a while, and then to go to Pale on the following day and to see Mr. Karadzic as agreed with him. And I don't know exactly when I was awakened; 5.00, 6.00, 7:00 in the morning, it has been a very long time since then, after all, but I remember very well my encounter and also what the reason was why somebody had awakened me, and that was more important for me to remember that rather than what time it was exactly. Namely, I left because somebody told me that Beara was trying to take people to the brick factory in order to possibly do something to them. Nobody said to me that he'd kill them there or something like that, but that was the assumption on the basis of his behaviour, and that is the kind of assumption that I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Deronjic. Then I did not link all of this up properly. You say now that you heard that Beara would take the people to the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So people were not already at the brick factory. The danger was that Beara would take them to the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you caught up with Beara, as you say yourself in your statement, you caught up with him at some kind of bridge that is halfway between Bratunac and the brick factory. He was alone. He was not bringing anyone along with him.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: He was on his own. He was in a car and I think that he had his escorts there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was not referring to his driver escorts or someone, but he was not bringing the prisoners along, none of them.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not see him with any prisoners. He was not taking anyone to the brick factory.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the result of your conversation with him then?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I asked him why he went to the brick factory, and I asked him what he intended to do there. He's not the manager of the brick factory in Bratunac. He went to the brick factory with a clear intention of doing something, to see what he could do to the prisoners. He said -- well, I'll try to remember his exact words as best I can. "Well, I went there to see whether perhaps some of the prisoners could be put up there." He did not say that he wanted to kill anyone there because he saw how worried I was about all of this. And I said to him, "Mr. Beara we talked about this last night. All of this is out of the question. The brick factory or anything else in Bratunac. Please go ahead and act on your orders but --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, on the basis of what you've been saying just now it is my understand that you did not want the prisoners to be kept in Bratunac. You wanted, regardless of whether they would be detained in the brick factory or some other facilities, you wanted them to be evacuated from Bratunac and to the military prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what you insisted upon, that Beara should do that, and that is what he accepted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ultimately that's what he did. And he did take these people in the area of -- in the direction of Zvornik the next day or, rather, that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 14th, he took them from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: The 14th. But I should just like to remind you of a fact. I think it's important, and that's why I refer to it. On the evening of the 13th, I received information that some buses, before Beara came to my office, had already set out - I don't know on whose orders, that is something I don't know at all - in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So this Beara who came to see you in the early morning of the 19th -- of the 14th, that was after midnight, actually. He had nothing to do with the people who were taken to Zvornik because he came to see you later.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, why do you preclude that possibility? And I'm sure that you are smart enough. He could have been in my office before too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking about what you could know.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was there before but there is such a possibility, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. According to the information that I have, Mr. Deronjic, you came to Pale on the 14th of July with a delegation from Srebrenica, is that right, for a meeting with Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: I will explain this to you, Mr. Milosevic. I explained this quite precisely in my longer text, and I expressed my doubts as to whether we held that meeting that day with the representatives from Srebrenica. Was it that day or perhaps the next day? I could not remember exactly. I thank you if you have this document. That means that it confirms that on that day we had that meeting too with the representatives from Srebrenica, who were opposed to my appointment as civilian commissioner, and they said that at a previous meeting. And I know on the 13th they went to see Karadzic, and they demanded that one of them be involved or appointed to the position that I had been appointed to. What am I trying to say now? I did not leave with the representatives of Srebrenica. I left the way I described this. I don't want to repeat it yet again. So there were two possibilities: The president and I perhaps met before that meeting if that meeting was on that day, with the representatives from Srebrenica; or there is this other possibility that perhaps on one of the following days this meeting was held with the representatives of Srebrenica. But at this meeting where I informed the president about these events, the people from Srebrenica were not present, although it is possible that on that day after that talk we also spoke to the representatives from Srebrenica. And I remember this meeting. I remember the details of the meeting with the representatives from Srebrenica, but I just wasn't sure whether this was after this meeting of mine with Karadzic or perhaps on one of the following days, because there was a great deal going on, and it's hard for me to remember each and everything exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have an excerpt here from the diary of the 14th of July. It says the 14th of July, but all of it is handwritten. Nevertheless, it can be read. I assume it's some plan, some schedule of meetings for that day, and it is my assumption that it was Karadzic's secretary who wrote this. I don't know. 1800 Churkin, and then 19 to 2240. And then it says Miraz or Mira Petrovic, 1315 to 1345, so that is half an hour. And then Karadzic and Ostojic, and then that was respond for the following day, and then 11:00 Deronjic Miroslav and the delegation from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not a document known to us, and obviously if the witness is to be asked about it, he should be shown copies of it, and it's a document obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's wait and see. We'll come to the point in a moment. Yes, go on, Mr. Milosevic, if you would get to the point, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is what the point is: This is a diary. This is an ordinary notebook of Karadzic's secretary, and my associates obtained this during the past few days. It says 1100 Deronjic Miroslav and delegation, "DLG" it says, of Srebrenica 11:00. But then in brackets it says 1425 until 1825. So on that day were you there with the delegation of Srebrenica for all of four hours with Karadzic? I'll give you this. You can have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see it. Before answering, he should be able to see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is in the second part, where it says the 14th of July. I have read all of this out to you in order. Perhaps it would be of assistance in terms of reconstructing what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what I see here is that it was envisaged, I imagine in this diary that you referred to, that Mr. Karadzic would meet with me at 11:00 in the morning of the 14th, and that the meeting with the representatives of Srebrenica would take place at 1425 until 1825.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. The only thing that it says there was that it was planned for the 11th but that it was held from 1425 until 1825, as it says in other cases when it was planned and when it actually took place. And for a variety of reasons, I cannot fathom this, but it's not for me to fathom it anyway. Did you spend four hours at Karadzic's with a delegation from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, look at this up here, Djoko Pudarevic [phoen] from 1520 to 1525. I'm not talking about the previous day. The date is behind it. It doesn't have to mean that it was actually held then, the meeting, but it was scheduled for then. But I am going to answer your question. I arrived in Pale, and I said it already and I cannot remember exactly at what time, and before that, President Karadzic and I were on our own. We held a meeting devoted to the subject of the events that had to do with the evacuation of civilians from Potocari. I think this is quite logical because it was the first time that we had the opportunity of meeting up again after the 12th, after the 13th, after the evacuation of Muslims from Potocari. And all the information that had to do with the meeting in Fontana, and so on and so forth, I had quite a few things to tell the president about. And during this part of the conversation, I conveyed to President Karadzic the details that I had at that moment related to the incidents in Konjevic Polje, about the large-scale massacre in Kravica at the cooperative in Kravica. I remember -- I recall that he asked me what happened to the bodies. That is something that remains in my memory. Then we also talked about Mr. Beara showing up in my office and I quoted the sentence that he conveyed to me verbatim, trying to find out what you are asking me about now all this time, whether this was his order or whether these were his instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've gone past the time for an adjournment. Can we see that document, please, Mr. Deronjic. Do you want to exhibit this photocopy, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be useful, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will simply mark it for identification, no more, because it's only a photocopy and the original is not present, but we could keep it marked for identification. Do you also want to exhibit the plea agreement you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll exhibit both those items.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the plea agreement will be Defence Exhibit 220, and this recent document will be Defence Exhibit 221 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we've considered the position about your cross-examination. You can have half an hour tomorrow morning further to continue your cross-examination of this witness. Mr. Deronjic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, I'm speaking to the witness. Mr. Deronjic, would you back, please, tomorrow morning at 9.00 to continue your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I absolutely cannot finish the cross-examination of this witness within half an hour. It is impossible.
